codes.meaning: The door isn't locking properly before the cycle can start.

F5 E2.what_it_means: The lid or door is not locking properly, so the machine will not begin the cycle.
F5 E2.why_it_happens: Something is stopping the latch seating -- laundry caught under the lid, a bent strike, or a lock mechanism that is wearing out.
F5 E2.what_to_try: Open and close the lid firmly with nothing caught in the opening, and check the strike and latch for anything obstructing them.
F5 E2.when_to_call: If the latch is clear and it still will not lock, the lid lock assembly is the usual culprit.

codes.meaning: The motor's speed sensor isn't reading correctly.
The machine isn't detecting enough incoming water flow.

F8 E1.what_it_means: The washer is not detecting enough incoming water flow. Some models display this as LO FL instead.
F8 E1.why_it_happens: Most often a supply tap that is not fully open, or an inlet screen behind the fill hoses that has silted up with scale and grit.
F8 E1.what_to_try: Check both hot and cold taps are fully open, then disconnect the fill hoses and look at the small screens in the inlet ports for debris.
F8 E1.when_to_call: If the supply is good and the screens are clean, the inlet valve on the machine needs checking.

LO FL.what_it_means: Low fill -- the washer is not seeing enough water coming in to run the cycle. The same condition as F8 E1 on models that show words rather than codes.
LO FL.why_it_happens: A partly closed supply tap or a blocked inlet screen, the same two causes as F8 E1.
LO FL.what_to_try: Confirm both taps are fully open and check the inlet screens behind the fill hoses.
LO FL.when_to_call: If supply and screens are both fine, the machine's inlet valve needs testing.

codes.meaning: Water is taking longer than about 8 minutes to drain.

F9 E1.what_it_means: The washer is taking longer than about eight minutes to drain, so it stops and reports a long drain.
F9 E1.why_it_happens: Usually a restriction rather than a failure -- a blocked drain hose, a standpipe that cannot take the flow, or debris in the pump.
F9 E1.what_to_try: Check the drain hose is not kinked and is not pushed more than a few inches into the standpipe, then check the pump filter if your model has an accessible one.
F9 E1.when_to_call: If the hose and standpipe are clear, the drain pump is the next thing to test.

codes.meaning: Too many suds have built up in the drum.

Sud.what_it_means: Too many suds have built up in the drum, so the washer pauses to let them clear. Displayed as Sd on some models.
Sud.why_it_happens: Usually too much detergent, or a non-HE detergent in a high-efficiency machine, which produces far more foam than the drum is designed to handle.
Sud.what_to_try: Let the cycle run its suds-clearing routine rather than interrupting it, then use less detergent next time and check it is HE-rated if your machine requires one.
Sud.when_to_call: If it appears with correct detergent and correct dosing, something is holding water in the drum and it is worth having checked.

Sd.what_it_means: The same excess-suds condition as Sud, shown as Sd on some displays.
Sd.why_it_happens: Too much detergent, or a non-HE detergent in a high-efficiency drum.
Sd.what_to_try: Let the suds-clearing routine run to the end, then reduce the dose on the next load and check the detergent is HE-rated.
Sd.when_to_call: If it appears with correct dosing, have the drain path checked.

codes.meaning: Not a fault — Control Lock is simply switched on.

LOC.what_it_means: Not a fault. Control Lock is switched on, so the buttons are deliberately ignoring input. Shown as LC on some models.
LOC.why_it_happens: It is usually turned on by accident, or on purpose to stop children changing a running cycle, and then forgotten.
LOC.what_to_try: Press and hold the Control Lock button -- often marked with a padlock, and sometimes a secondary function of another button -- for a few seconds to release it.
LOC.when_to_call: Only if the lock will not release, which points at the control panel rather than the setting.

codes.meaning: The washer cannot detect a detergent cartridge loaded in the dispenser.
Not a fault — the cycle was paused or cancelled and the machine is unwinding it.
Items were left in the drum during a Clean Washer cycle, which has to run empty.
A problem in the dispenser system, so detergent or softener is not being released.
The fridge is flagging that it lost power long enough for the freezer compartment to climb to 18°F or warmer.
The control board has caught an internal fault it can't self-correct and is asking for a power cycle.
A blinking 'F' alone is the control board's generic signal that something is wrong internally, before it narrows to a specific fault.
An undercounter unit's control has logged a fault it wants cleared with a power-down reset.
Same family as E1 on undercounter refrigerators.
The cabinet temperature has drifted outside its acceptable range in one direction or the other.
Moisture has pooled in the tray underneath the tub, which the machine reads as a possible leak.
The valve that lets water into the machine is being commanded but isn't responding electrically.
The motor that drives the wash/spray arm isn't performing as expected during a cycle.
A cycle is taking far longer than normal to drain out the used wash water.
The main control board and the user-facing interface aren't communicating properly.
The valve that routes water between the upper and lower spray arms isn't switching correctly.
The oven's electronic control has hit a problem it can't categorize into one of its known fault types.
The temperature sensor in the lower oven cavity, or its wiring, is likely at fault.
The oven's main appliance-management control board itself appears to be the source of the problem.
On combination wall ovens with a built-in microwave, this points to the microwave's inverter or magnetron tube rather than the oven side.
The keypad/user interface panel or its connection to the main control is suspected.
The oven door's latch assembly or the switch that senses whether the door is latched isn't behaving as expected.
The range's electronic control has encountered a fault it can't identify as a specific known type.
The main oven's temperature sensor — or the warming drawer's sensor, on models equipped with one — is the suspected cause.
The main oven door's latch assembly or door switch appears to be malfunctioning.
The door latch or the switch that confirms the door is locked (used during self-clean) is likely at fault.
The range's main control board, keypad, or user interface is the suspected source of the fault.
Often triggered by a burner grate sitting in the wrong spot on a sensor/switch; if grates are fine, it points to the control/keypad.
Power to the unit was interrupted long enough that the freezer compartment warmed to 18°F or higher, so it's flagging that frozen food may be at risk.
The fresh-food side has stayed above 48°F, or the freezer side above 15°F, for more than about 90 minutes — a sustained warming event rather than a brief door opening.
A power blip during the cycle — not a hardware fault — interrupted the dryer mid-run.

PF.what_it_means: Not a fault. A power interruption stopped the cycle partway and the dryer is reporting it.
PF.why_it_happens: An outage, a tripped breaker, or the plug being pulled mid-cycle.
PF.what_to_try: Restart the cycle. If it keeps happening with no outage you can account for, check the breaker and that the dryer is not sharing an overloaded circuit.
PF.when_to_call: If PF recurs with a stable supply, the power board is worth checking.

codes.meaning: The dryer isn't getting enough incoming line voltage to power its heating element, even though the drum may keep tumbling.
Airflow through the dryer is restricted, almost always from a clogged lint screen or a crushed, kinked, or overly long vent run.
The user-interface control panel or its wiring is the likely source of the fault.
The moisture sensor has failed to register any moisture reading across five dry cycles in a row.
Any alternating letter/number pair beginning with F not otherwise documented is the control board's way of flagging a service-level fault.
That cooking zone's surface is still hot to the touch, even picked up from a neighboring zone or a hot pan set on it.
The cooktop isn't detecting a compatible pot on an induction zone — wrong material, poor centering, or too small a pan.
The electronics underneath the cooktop have gotten too hot internally, so the unit shuts the zone off as a protective measure.
The touchpad/user-interface panel or its wiring is the suspected fault location.
Same general area as FC E1 — the touchpad interface or its associated wiring is implicated.
The right-front cooking element/hotplate or its wiring is pointed to as the problem.
